title: Weather Chart and Seasonal Changes
strapline: A symbol added every morning — and by half-term, a real record of a season changing.
intent: Children recognise changes in the environment as spring begins.
A daily chart builds the habit of observing and recording, day after day.
Children connect weather to real decisions — what we wear, whether we go out.
Reading the chart back is early data handling: which was the commonest weather?
A shared daily routine gives the day a predictable, settling shape.
implementation: Create a daily weather chart with symbols children add themselves for sun, rain, cloud, wind.
Make it a fixed part of the morning routine, run by a different child each day.
Go and look out of the window or step outside rather than guessing indoors.
Discuss how the weather affects what we wear and what we can do today.
Extend vocabulary deliberately: rainy, cloudy, sunny, frosty, breezy, warm, cool.
Link the chart to the children's own experiences — puddles on the way in, cold hands.
Count up the symbols at the end of each week and talk about what the chart shows.
key_questions: What is the weather doing today? How can you tell?
What will you need to wear to go outside?
How many sunny days have we had this week?
Which weather have we had most of? Which least?
What has changed outside since the winter?

impact.text: Children notice weather and seasons and what they mean for us.
Children observe and describe change in their environment over time.
Children count and compare amounts, reading a simple record back.
Children take up specific weather vocabulary and use it themselves.
Children follow the room's daily rhythms and help run them.
Children know what their body needs — warmth, a coat, a drink — and act on it.

enhancements: A real rain gauge and windsock the children read and empty themselves.
A seasonal photo of the same tree taken every fortnight from the same spot.
A dressing-the-bear activity where the clothes must match today's chart.
A weather song or rhyme sung as the symbol goes up.
A block graph built from the week's symbols to compare at a glance.
A puddle investigation on a wet day — measure it, come back, measure again.

playing_exploring: Children go out and investigate the weather with their own senses.
The chart is theirs to run, so the routine belongs to them.
active_learning: Children keep the record going every single day across a half-term.
They take the job seriously and remind adults when it is missed.
creating_thinking: Children read the chart back and draw conclusions from it.
They link weather to consequences — what we wear, what we can do.
